idiom_name: rayon::join / par_iter on the Rayon work-stealing pool
implementation_notes: Rayon is the standard fork/join runtime for Rust: rayon::join(a, b) forks two closures and joins them, par_iter/par_sort/par_reduce cover bulk work, and the global pool schedules tasks with work stealing at very low overhead (the docs describe the mechanism explicitly). The borrow checker shapes the decomposition the pattern wants: sibling tasks must own or borrow disjoint pieces (split_at, split_at_mut, chunks_mut), which rules out the shared-mutable-state mistakes fork/join suffers elsewhere. std::thread::scope (Rust 1.63) provides a dependency-free scoped join for shallow, balanced splits; rayon stays the default for sustained or irregular parallel workloads.
pitfalls: Rayon closures must be Send: share data through disjoint borrows (split_at/split_at_mut) or moved ownership, never through aliased &mut or RefCell.
Blocking inside join/par_iter (I/O, locks, channel waits) stalls the pool and can deadlock - the join documentation warns about exactly this; use async/tokio for waiting work.
Panics propagate from the first failing closure and the sibling still runs (join guarantees both execute), so side effects before the join cannot be assumed atomic.

variants.name: std::thread::scope + manual split/join (no dependencies)
variants.implementation_notes: Without a library, std::thread::scope spawns threads that may borrow stack data and are guaranteed to be joined before the scope returns - a correct fork/join for shallow, balanced splits. There is no pool, no queue and no stealing, so the recursion depth is the thread count: threshold hard (or cap the depth) and use it for two-way splits of large inputs, not for irregular trees. Choose it when adding a runtime dependency is unacceptable and the workload is embarrassingly parallel.
pitfalls: One OS thread per split is expensive: without a pool the thread count is your responsibility, and a missing threshold creates thousands of threads.
No stealing: an unbalanced split leaves cores idle, and a panicking spawned thread surfaces only at the join (scope panics on exit if a thread panicked).
Scoped borrows are checked: siblings must take disjoint borrows or the closures do not compile.
